screens.narratorSegment: In this session you'll learn how Snowflake makes semi-structured data practical and fast. We will focus on the VARIANT data type, which holds JSON, AVRO, or XML in a parsed, internal format so you can query fields without rigid, pre-defined tables. You'll see how to stage files and use COPY INTO to load JSON into a VARIANT column, how to access values with dot and bracket notation, and how to normalize nested arrays using the FLATTEN function. We will also cover useful helper functions, like TRY_PARSE_JSON for handling malformed input, and performance ideas such as extracting frequently filtered fields into typed columns. Think of VARIANT as a flexible container that lets you treat messy A P I or log output like first-class analytic data while still avoiding full table rewrites. As you explore, notice patterns you can reuse: stage, copy, query, flatten, and optionally extract into typed columns for speed.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Working with Semi‑Structured Data
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Live coding orientation

Working with Semi‑Structured Data

Learn how Snowflake stores JSON, AVRO, and XML in VARIANT columns, how to load files with COPY INTO, and how to query and normalize nested data for analytics.

In this lesson
Store semi-structured payloads in VARIANT and query fields whenever you need them. Avoid rigid schema changes.
Why it matters
APIs, logs, and IoT output often arrive as JSON. VARIANT lets analysts query that data with SQL without losing flexibility.
Outcome
Extract nested fields, flatten arrays to rows, and decide which fields should become typed columns for performance.
Common pitfall
Relying on ad hoc parsing for frequently filtered fields rather than extracting them into typed columns.
Explore Key Topics
VARIANT data type
Parsed, columnar storage for semi-structured payloads enables schema-on-read.
Loading with COPY INTO
Stage files, then COPY INTO to place objects into VARIANT or typed columns during load.
FLATTEN
Explode nested arrays into rows so SQL can analyze each element naturally.
Concept map
VARIANT
One column stores JSON/AVRO/XML in parsed form for fast queries.
Dot & Bracket Notation
Access nested keys and array elements easily in SQL.
FLATTEN
Turn arrays into rows so analytics can aggregate per element.
This lesson follows a live-coding flow: show sample file, create table, copy data, query with notation and functions, then normalize nested arrays.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: We will focus on four practical skills that turn semi-structured data into analyzable tables. First, you will understand the VARIANT data type: what it stores and why Snowflake keeps semi-structured payloads in an internal parsed format. Knowing this helps you avoid unnecessary parsing work and use Snowflake efficiently. Second, you'll learn how to load JSON, AVRO, or XML into Snowflake using staging and COPY INTO. This includes extracting fields into typed columns during the load, which is critical when you want fast filters. Third, you'll be able to query nested fields with dot and bracket notation and the suite of helper functions Snowflake provides. That skill means you can work with nested payloads using familiar S Q L patterns. Fourth, you'll apply the FLATTEN table function to explode nested arrays into rows for relational analysis. Flattening is essential when you want to aggregate or join on elements inside arrays. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you’ve achieved it.

screens.title: What is VARIANT and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: VARIANT is a special Snowflake column type that can hold any semi-structured payload, such as JSON, AVRO, or XML, in a parsed internal format. The key idea is that Snowflake does the parsing at load time into an optimized columnar representation, so when you query nested fields later, the system can operate efficiently without needing to reparse text for every query. A practical example: an events feed from an A P I might include user properties and nested details; storing that payload in VARIANT preserves the entire object while letting you extract only the fields you need for a report. A common misconception is to treat VARIANT as an opaque blob and avoid casting or extracting fields; while VARIANT keeps the full structure, explicitly casting frequently used fields to S Q L types during load or transformation ensures correct types and better performance. Another subtle point: you do not need to call JSON parsing functions on data already stored as VARIANT — it is already parsed. The takeaway is that VARIANT gives you schema-on-read flexibility without sacrificing many performance benefits of columnar storage. Ask yourself: which fields will you query often and should therefore be promoted to typed columns?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › What is VARIANT
Definition
VARIANT is a Snowflake column type that stores semi-structured data parsed into an internal, columnar format. It preserves full objects while allowing field-level access and casts.
Analogy
Think of VARIANT as a smart container: you keep the whole package but can pull individual parts on demand without unpacking the entire box every time.
Example
An event payload from an API with nested details is stored in VARIANT so analysts can query user_id, action, or nested device info without schema migration.
Key Takeaway

VARIANT preserves a parsed object for flexible queries; promote hot fields to typed columns when you need fast filters.

Why this matters
  • Enables schema-on-read: you decide which parts of the structure matter when you query.
  • Avoids repeated parsing costs because Snowflake stores a parsed representation.
  • Allows you to keep the raw structure for audits or reprocessing while using typed fields for frequent queries.
Misconception
Storing everything in VARIANT and never extracting fields is convenient but can lead to slower filters. Extract commonly used fields to typed columns instead.

screens.title: Loading semi-structured files with COPY INTO
screens.narratorSegment: Loading semi-structured files starts with a stage and ends with a table that either contains a VARIANT column or typed columns populated from fields inside the payload. First create an internal stage and upload your JSON file. Then create a table with a VARIANT column; you may add typed columns for fields you expect to filter on often. When you run COPY INTO, use a SELECT from the stage where you extract fields using the field path notation and casts. For example, select the staged record, extract user_id and timestamp and cast them to INT and TIMESTAMP, and put the entire object into the VARIANT column. This approach both preserves the raw object and makes key fields available as typed columns for efficient filtering. A practical tip: use FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON) so Snowflake knows how to interpret staged files. If you have potentially malformed JSON strings, wrap them with TRY_PARSE_JSON during the load to avoid failing the entire COPY INTO. Finally, validate by running a sample query to confirm typed columns match expectations. Would any of your pipelines benefit from extracting a few hot fields at load time?

keyIdea.title: Load process
keyIdea.text: Stage files, then use COPY INTO with a SELECT that extracts fields and casts types while storing the full object in VARIANT.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Loading with COPY INTO
Step-by-step
1. Create a stage and upload files
Use an internal or external stage and upload JSON, AVRO, or XML files for COPY INTO.
2. Create a table with VARIANT
Add VARIANT for raw payloads and typed columns for hot fields you will filter on frequently.
3. COPY INTO using SELECT
Select fields from staged records, cast them, and place the record into the VARIANT column.
4. Validate and handle malformed rows
Use TRY_PARSE_JSON if records may be invalid so COPY INTO completes and problematic rows can be inspected later.
Key Takeaway

Extract and cast hot fields during load to speed filters, while storing the full object in VARIANT for flexibility.

COPY INTO example
-- Create a table with a VARIANT column
CREATE TABLE raw_events (
  event_id INT,
  event_timestamp TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
  event_data VARIANT
);

-- Load JSON and extract fields
COPY INTO raw_events (event_id, event_timestamp, event_data)
FROM (
  SELECT
    $1:user_id::INT,
    $1:timestamp::TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
    $1
  FROM @my_json_stage/events.json
)
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON);
This example extracts user_id and timestamp while preserving the entire object. Use TRY_PARSE_JSON when input may be a malformed JSON string.

screens.title: Extracting fields during load and casting types
screens.narratorSegment: When you extract values from a staged semi-structured record, explicit casting makes your intent clear and prevents type surprises. During COPY INTO, you can use the staged column reference and pathing to pull a field and immediately cast it to the desired S Q L type. For instance, extract a user identifier and cast to INT, or take a timestamp string and cast to TIMESTAMP_NTZ. This step ensures downstream queries see the right data types and that clustering or pruning based on these columns works. A simple example: select the first staged column's user_id field and cast it to integer while also keeping the full object in VARIANT. A common misconception is to rely on automatic inference; while Snowflake does infer in many cases, explicit casting prevents unexpected nulls or string comparisons in filters. Also, when records might contain malformed JSON strings, wrap parsing with TRY_PARSE_JSON before casting so malformed rows produce null values rather than failing. As a validation step run a sample SELECT after COPY INTO to confirm typed columns contain expected values. Could any of your ingestion jobs benefit from adding explicit casts at load time?

keyIdea.title: Casting rule
keyIdea.text: Always cast extracted VARIANT values to the intended SQL type during load or transformation to ensure correct behavior and performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Casting during load
Example load with casting
COPY INTO raw_events (event_id, event_timestamp, event_data)
FROM (
  SELECT
    $1:user_id::INT,
    $1:timestamp::TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
    $1
  FROM @my_json_stage/events.json
)
FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON);
This SELECT extracts and casts user_id and timestamp while storing the full JSON into event_data. Casting here prevents later surprises and supports pruning when queried.
Checks and tips
  • Run a sample SELECT on staged records to confirm paths before COPY INTO.
  • Use TRY_PARSE_JSON if the staged content might be raw strings containing JSON.
  • Promote fields you filter on to typed columns to enable pruning and indexes to work.
Common mistake
Relying on implicit type inference can return unexpected types or nulls in downstream queries.

screens.title: Dot notation vs. Bracket notation
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake supports two common ways to access elements inside a VARIANT: dot notation and bracket notation. Dot notation uses a colon to separate the column name and the key, similar to object access in many languages, and reads naturally for standard keys with no special characters. Bracket notation uses square brackets and is necessary when key names contain spaces, dashes, or other characters that dot notation cannot reference cleanly. Bracket notation is also how you index arrays by numeric position. For example, use dot style to get a simple user_id field, and bracket style when a key has a hyphen or when you need the first element of an items array. A common misconception is that bracket notation is slower; performance depends on how you use the extracted value and whether you cast it. Another trap is incorrect pathing: using the wrong sequence of keys will return null. When you choose notation, prefer readability for maintenance but switch to bracket notation when keys require it. As a quick test, try both styles on your sample data to confirm they return the same value for simple keys, and use bracket indexing when you need array elements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Notation Comparison
Dot notation (simple keys)
Example: access a top-level key called user_id using the column, a colon, and the key name, then cast to the desired type.
When to use
Readable and concise when keys are simple and stable.
Pro tip
If you control the producer, prefer simple keys so dot notation can be used consistently.
Bracket notation (special keys & arrays)
Example: use bracket notation when keys have spaces or punctuation, or when you need to access an array element by index.
When to use
Necessary for special-character keys and for indexing arrays like items[0].
Common mistake
Mixing notations incorrectly or using the wrong path sequence returns null. Verify paths against sample records first.

screens.title: Key helper functions for VARIANT
screens.narratorSegment: Snowflake provides a set of functions tailored for semi-structured data. GET and GET_PATH let you retrieve values when you prefer function-style access rather than notation. PARSE_JSON converts a text string into a VARIANT value; use it when you start with a VARCHAR that contains JSON text. TRY_PARSE_JSON behaves the same but returns null instead of throwing an error when parsing fails, and this is invaluable during bulk loads that may include malformed rows. ARRAY_SIZE returns the number of elements in an array within a VARIANT, while OBJECT_KEYS lists the keys of an object. TO_JSON converts a VARIANT back into a textual JSON representation when needed. A concrete example: if you have a column that sometimes contains raw JSON as a string, wrap it in TRY_PARSE_JSON inside COPY INTO so bad rows become null and the load continues. A common misconception is calling PARSE_JSON on data already stored as VARIANT; that is unnecessary and redundant. Learn to match the function to the input type: use PARSE_JSON or TRY_PARSE_JSON on VARCHAR, and use GET or path notation on VARIANT. What parsing functions might help tidy up your incoming feeds?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Helper Functions
PARSE_JSON / TRY_PARSE_JSON
Convert VARCHAR JSON text to VARIANT. TRY_PARSE_JSON returns null for malformed input so loads can continue.
GET / GET_PATH
Function-style access to object keys or nested paths when you prefer functions over notation.
ARRAY_SIZE / OBJECT_KEYS
Inspect array lengths and object key lists so you can validate structure before flattening or aggregating.
Practical pattern
When ingesting, use TRY_PARSE_JSON on any VARCHAR inputs that may contain JSON. Use ARRAY_SIZE to guard FLATTEN calls and avoid unnecessary lateral joins on empty arrays.
Key Takeaway

Match the function to the input: parse text to VARIANT with TRY_PARSE_JSON, then inspect or extract with GET, GET_PATH, or notation.

screens.title: Using FLATTEN to normalize nested arrays
screens.narratorSegment: FLATTEN is a table function that explodes arrays or objects stored in VARIANT into rows so you can analyze each element as if it were its own record. The typical pattern uses LATERAL FLATTEN with the input set to a VARIANT array path; this returns a value column that represents each array element. For example, if orders include an items array, FLATTEN(input => order_data:items) produces rows where each row's item. value holds the element. You then extract fields like product and qty from item. value and join or aggregate as needed. A concrete example: given an order with two items, FLATTEN produces two rows for that order, enabling per-item revenue calculations. Watch out for empty arrays: FLATTEN on an empty array yields no rows, which may drop the parent record if not handled; you can guard with ARRAY_SIZE > 0 or use OUTER joins. Another subtlety: always reference the FLATTEN alias's value field when extracting element attributes. The practical question to consider is how you will re-associate flattened rows back to the parent — include the parent id to preserve context.

keyIdea.title: Flatten purpose
keyIdea.text: FLATTEN explodes arrays into rows using LATERAL so you can aggregate and join on individual elements.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Using FLATTEN
FLATTEN example
SELECT
  o.event_id,
  o.event_timestamp,
  item.value:id::INT AS item_id,
  item.value:qty::INT AS quantity
FROM
  raw_events AS o,
  LATERAL FLATTEN(input => o.event_data:items) AS item;
Here item.value is each array element. Cast nested fields to proper types and include the parent id so you can re-link items back to their order or event.
Notes & caveats
  • FLATTEN on empty arrays returns no rows; guard with ARRAY_SIZE or use an OUTER lateral approach.
  • Always include parent keys when flattening so context is preserved for joins and aggregations.
  • Deeply nested arrays may need staged or iterative flattening steps to normalize fully.
Common mistake
Forgetting to re-attach the parent id leads to orphaned rows that are hard to reconcile.

screens.title: Flattening an orders example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete orders example to make flattening tangible. Suppose each order record contains an items array with objects for product, quantity, and price. When you store orders in a VARIANT column, you can use LATERAL FLATTEN to convert the items array into multiple rows, one per item. In practice you write a SELECT that joins the original table with LATERAL FLATTEN(input => orders_raw:items) and alias the result as item. Then extract item. value:product, item. value:qty, and item. value:price, casting types as needed. This lets you compute per-item revenue and aggregate totals across orders with standard GROUP BY. Consider empty arrays: if an order has no items, FLATTEN will produce zero rows for that order; to keep the order row, test ARRAY_SIZE or use an OUTER FLATTEN pattern. A misconception to avoid is assuming FLATTEN automatically preserves parent rows; it does not. Finally, to validate the result, run a GROUP BY on order_id and compare sum of item price times qty with the original order total, if present. How will you ensure correctness when importing your first nested dataset?

Finally, to validate the result, run a GROUP BY on order_id and compare sum of item price times qty with the original order total, if present. keyIdea.title: Practical flatten
keyIdea.text: Explode nested items into rows with LATERAL FLATTEN, cast extracted fields, and re-link to parent order_id for aggregation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Orders Flatten Example
Example query
SELECT
  o.order_data:order_id::INT AS order_id,
  item.value:product::VARCHAR AS product_name,
  item.value:qty::INT AS quantity,
  item.value:price::DECIMAL(10,2) AS unit_price
FROM
  orders_raw o,
  LATERAL FLATTEN(input => o.order_data:items) AS item;
This produces one row per item with the parent order_id, allowing you to compute revenue per product or join items to a product master table.
Validation checks
  • Compare aggregate item totals with an order-level total, if available.
  • Guard against empty arrays by checking ARRAY_SIZE before flattening if you want to preserve parent rows.
  • Include order_id in the flattened output so results remain joinable back to the source table.
Key Takeaway

Flatten to analyze elements, but always carry the parent id and validate aggregates to ensure correctness.

screens.title: Performance considerations and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Working with VARIANT gives flexibility, but there are performance trade-offs to consider. Querying deeply nested fields directly in VARIANT is convenient, but if you frequently filter on those fields, Snowflake may need to scan more data. The best practice is to extract fields you filter or join on into strongly typed columns during load or transformation. That allows pruning and reduces compute for repeated queries. Another practical tip is to avoid excessive nested complexity in production queries — if you repeatedly access the same nested path, extract it once and store it as a column. Also, watch out for deep nesting causing complex plans; flattening during ETL can simplify downstream analytics. A common misconception is that storing everything in VARIANT eliminates the need for schema design — it doesn't. Think of VARIANT as a bridge: use it for ingest flexibility, then normalize hot fields for performance. Finally, monitor query profiles and consider materialized views or clustered tables when you have expensive joins on flattened results. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Performance & Best Practices
When to extract fields

  • High-cardinality fields that drive pruning are good candidates for extraction.
  • Keep VARIANT for less-used or audit-oriented data.
ETL vs. query-time flattening
If array elements are regularly analyzed, normalize during ETL so queries are simpler and faster. Use FLATTEN in scheduled transformations when necessary.
Operational tips
Monitor query profiles and costs. If certain nested paths create expensive plans, extract them or precompute results. Consider materialized views for repeated heavy aggregations on flattened data.
Key Takeaway

Use VARIANT for flexible ingestion and typed columns for query performance. Balance flexibility with the cost of repeated parsing or full scans.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and debugging tips
screens.narratorSegment: Several common mistakes recur when working with semi-structured data. First, incorrect pathing — using the wrong key names or ordering — will silently return nulls when you expect values. Always inspect a sample record to confirm paths. Second, unnecessary parsing: applying PARSE_JSON to data that is already a VARIANT is redundant and wastes compute. Third, empty arrays: FLATTEN on an empty array yields no rows, which may cause missing parent records if you forget to handle that case. Fourth, malformed JSON strings: if staged files include badly formed JSON, COPY INTO can fail; use TRY_PARSE_JSON to convert errors into null values and let the load continue so you can purge or fix bad rows later. Debugging tips include running SELECTs against staged content before COPY INTO, using ARRAY_SIZE and OBJECT_KEYS to inspect structure, and comparing aggregates pre- and post-flatten to ensure you haven't lost data. When you spot unexpected nulls, recheck your path strings and consider running TRY_PARSE_JSON or a sample PARSE to see where parsing fails. fullNarratorScript:
In this session you'll learn how Snowflake makes semi-structured data practical and fast. We will focus on the VARIANT data type, which holds JSON, AVRO, or XML in a parsed, internal format so you can query fields without rigid, pre-defined tables. You'll see how to stage files and use COPY INTO to load JSON into a VARIANT column, how to access values with dot and bracket notation, and how to normalize nested arrays using the FLATTEN function. We will also cover useful helper functions, like TRY_PARSE_JSON for handling malformed input, and performance ideas such as extracting frequently filtered fields into typed columns. By the end you should be comfortable loading semi-structured files, querying nested fields safely, and turning arrays into rows for relational analysis. Think of VARIANT as a flexible container that lets you treat messy A P I or log output like first-class analytic data while still avoiding full table rewrites. As you explore, notice patterns you can reuse: stage, copy, query, flatten, and optionally extract into typed columns for speed.

We will focus on four practical skills that turn semi-structured data into analyzable tables. First, you will understand the VARIANT data type: what it stores and why Snowflake keeps semi-structured payloads in an internal parsed format. Knowing this helps you avoid unnecessary parsing work and use Snowflake efficiently. Second, you'll learn how to load JSON, AVRO, or XML into Snowflake using staging and COPY INTO. This includes extracting fields into typed columns during the load, which is critical when you want fast filters. Third, you'll be able to query nested fields with dot and bracket notation and the suite of helper functions Snowflake provides. That skill means you can work with nested payloads using familiar S Q L patterns. Fourth, you'll apply the FLATTEN table function to explode nested arrays into rows for relational analysis. Flattening is essential when you want to aggregate or join on elements inside arrays. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you know when you’ve achieved it.

On this page we add practical framing so you can practice safely. You will learn to stage files and use COPY INTO with explicit casts to avoid type surprises during ingestion. Practice using TRY_PARSE_JSON when you suspect malformed input so loads won't fail. Work with dot notation for stable key names and bracket notation when keys have special characters or when you index arrays. When you flatten arrays, check for empty arrays and nulls so your joins and aggregates stay correct. Finally, practice extracting high‑cardinality or frequently filtered fields into typed columns during load or transformation to allow pruning and better performance. Each practice area includes a milestone that verifies you handled malformed records, extracted key fields, and normalized nested arrays without data loss. These safety steps prevent full table scans and save compute. Try the hands-on activity at the end of the chapter to reinforce these methods.

VARIANT is a special Snowflake column type that can hold any semi-structured payload, such as JSON, AVRO, or XML, in a parsed internal format. The key idea is that Snowflake does the parsing at load time into an optimized columnar representation, so when you query nested fields later, the system can operate efficiently without needing to reparse text for every query. A practical example: an events feed from an A P I might include user properties and nested details; storing that payload in VARIANT preserves the entire object while letting you extract only the fields you need for a report. A common misconception is to treat VARIANT as an opaque blob and avoid casting or extracting fields; while VARIANT keeps the full structure, explicitly casting frequently used fields to S Q L types during load or transformation ensures correct types and better performance. Another subtle point: you do not need to call JSON parsing functions on data already stored as VARIANT — it is already parsed. The takeaway is that VARIANT gives you schema-on-read flexibility without sacrificing many performance benefits of columnar storage. Ask yourself: which fields will you query often and should therefore be promoted to typed columns?

Loading semi-structured files starts with a stage and ends with a table that either contains a VARIANT column or typed columns populated from fields inside the payload. First create an internal stage and upload your JSON file. Then create a table with a VARIANT column; you may add typed columns for fields you expect to filter on often. When you run COPY INTO, use a SELECT from the stage where you extract fields using the field path notation and casts. For example, select the staged record, extract user_id and timestamp and cast them to INT and TIMESTAMP, and put the entire object into the VARIANT column. This approach both preserves the raw object and makes key fields available as typed columns for efficient filtering. A practical tip: use FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON) so Snowflake knows how to interpret staged files. If you have potentially malformed JSON strings, wrap them with TRY_PARSE_JSON during the load to avoid failing the entire COPY INTO. Finally, validate by running a sample query to confirm typed columns match expectations. Would any of your pipelines benefit from extracting a few hot fields at load time?

When you extract values from a staged semi-structured record, explicit casting makes your intent clear and prevents type surprises. During COPY INTO, you can use the staged column reference and pathing to pull a field and immediately cast it to the desired S Q L type. For instance, extract a user identifier and cast to INT, or take a timestamp string and cast to TIMESTAMP_NTZ. This step ensures downstream queries see the right data types and that clustering or pruning based on these columns works. A simple example: select the first staged column's user_id field and cast it to integer while also keeping the full object in VARIANT. A common misconception is to rely on automatic inference; while Snowflake does infer in many cases, explicit casting prevents unexpected nulls or string comparisons in filters. Also, when records might contain malformed JSON strings, wrap parsing with TRY_PARSE_JSON before casting so malformed rows produce null values rather than failing. As a validation step run a sample SELECT after COPY INTO to confirm typed columns contain expected values. Could any of your ingestion jobs benefit from adding explicit casts at load time?

Snowflake supports two common ways to access elements inside a VARIANT: dot notation and bracket notation. Dot notation uses a colon to separate the column name and the key, similar to object access in many languages, and reads naturally for standard keys with no special characters. Bracket notation uses square brackets and is necessary when key names contain spaces, dashes, or other characters that dot notation cannot reference cleanly. Bracket notation is also how you index arrays by numeric position. For example, use dot style to get a simple user_id field, and bracket style when a key has a hyphen or when you need the first element of an items array. A common misconception is that bracket notation is slower; performance depends on how you use the extracted value and whether you cast it. Another trap is incorrect pathing: using the wrong sequence of keys will return null. When you choose notation, prefer readability for maintenance but switch to bracket notation when keys require it. As a quick test, try both styles on your sample data to confirm they return the same value for simple keys, and use bracket indexing when you need array elements.

Snowflake provides a set of functions tailored for semi-structured data. GET and GET_PATH let you retrieve values when you prefer function-style access rather than notation. PARSE_JSON converts a text string into a VARIANT value; use it when you start with a VARCHAR that contains JSON text. TRY_PARSE_JSON behaves the same but returns null instead of throwing an error when parsing fails, and this is invaluable during bulk loads that may include malformed rows. ARRAY_SIZE returns the number of elements in an array within a VARIANT, while OBJECT_KEYS lists the keys of an object. TO_JSON converts a VARIANT back into a textual JSON representation when needed. A concrete example: if you have a column that sometimes contains raw JSON as a string, wrap it in TRY_PARSE_JSON inside COPY INTO so bad rows become null and the load continues. A common misconception is calling PARSE_JSON on data already stored as VARIANT; that is unnecessary and redundant. Learn to match the function to the input type: use PARSE_JSON or TRY_PARSE_JSON on VARCHAR, and use GET or path notation on VARIANT. What parsing functions might help tidy up your incoming feeds?

FLATTEN is a table function that explodes arrays or objects stored in VARIANT into rows so you can analyze each element as if it were its own record. The typical pattern uses LATERAL FLATTEN with the input set to a VARIANT array path; this returns a value column that represents each array element. For example, if orders include an items array, FLATTEN(input => order_data:items) produces rows where each row's item. value holds the element. You then extract fields like product and qty from item. value and join or aggregate as needed. A concrete example: given an order with two items, FLATTEN produces two rows for that order, enabling per-item revenue calculations. Watch out for empty arrays: FLATTEN on an empty array yields no rows, which may drop the parent record if not handled; you can guard with ARRAY_SIZE > 0 or use OUTER joins. Another subtlety: always reference the FLATTEN alias's value field when extracting element attributes. The practical question to consider is how you will re-associate flattened rows back to the parent — include the parent id to preserve context.

Let's walk through a concrete orders example to make flattening tangible. Suppose each order record contains an items array with objects for product, quantity, and price. When you store orders in a VARIANT column, you can use LATERAL FLATTEN to convert the items array into multiple rows, one per item. A few final concepts tie operations together. Bracket notation accesses keys with special characters and indexes arrays. FLATTEN with LATERAL explodes arrays into rows so you can analyze each element as its own record. COPY INTO is the canonical way to load staged semi-structured files; during the load you can extract and cast fields to make queries efficient. TRY_PARSE_JSON is a safety net that returns null for malformed JSON strings, letting loads continue while you address bad rows. Finally, always validate counts and aggregates after flatten operations to ensure you didn't lose parent rows due to empty arrays.
